direct_answer: Compression stockings need a firm pull, which can be very hard with painful, stiff hands. Stocking applicators, rubber gloves, zips or wraps may help, and a nurse, pharmacist or occupational therapist can advise. Do not stop prescribed compression without checking with whoever prescribed it.

content:
Compression stockings are often prescribed for leg swelling, varicose veins or to help prevent blood clots. They are deliberately tight, so pulling them on can be hard when hand osteoarthritis affects your grip.

This guide covers practical options for managing compression stockings with painful hands. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Why they can be hard with hand osteoarthritis

  • They need strong pinch and grip to pull up.
  • Bending to reach your feet may be hard if hips, knees or back are stiff.
  • Hands are often stiffest in the morning, when stockings are usually put on.

Things that may help

  • Ask about a stocking applicator (donning aid) or a slippery sock-style aid.
  • Wearing rubber gloves gives better grip and spreads the pull.
  • Put stockings on soon after getting up, before swelling builds, once hands have warmed up.
  • Turn the stocking inside out down to the heel, then roll it up gradually.
  • Sit down in a stable chair with armrests.

Alternatives to ask about

  • Different compression classes, styles or sizes.
  • Stockings with zips or open toes.
  • Adjustable wrap systems with Velcro.
  • Help from a carer, district nurse or care worker.

Who can help

Talk to the nurse, GP or pharmacist who prescribed or supplied the stockings, and ask for an occupational therapy assessment if dressing is generally getting hard. Stockings should be measured and fitted properly, and checked for skin problems.

When to get help

  • Call 999 if you have chest pain or sudden breathlessness.
  • Get urgent advice from NHS 111 or your GP if one leg becomes suddenly swollen, red, warm or painful, as this can be a sign of a blood clot.
  • Remove stockings and seek advice if your toes become numb, pale, blue or very painful, or you notice broken skin.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Can I just stop wearing them?

Do not stop prescribed compression without speaking to the person who prescribed it. There may be other options.

Do stocking aids work with weak hands?

Many people find them helpful. An OT can suggest which type suits you.
